'''3.''' To furnish with a bolster in dress; pad; stuff out with padding.
{{smaller block|Three pair of stays ''bolstered'' below the left shoulder.

'''bolsterer''' (bōl′stėr-ėr), ''n.'' One who bolsters; a supporter.

'''bolstering''' (bōl′stėr-ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''bolster'', ''v.''] A prop or support; padding.

'''bolster-plate''' (bōl′stėr-plāt), ''n.'' An iron plate placed on the under side of the bolster of a wagon, to serve as a wearing surface.

'''bolster-spring''' (bōl′stėr-spring), ''n.'' A spring placed on the beam of a car-truck, to support the bolster and the body of the car.

'''bolster-work''' (bōl′stėr-wėrk), ''n.'' Architectural features, or courses of masonry, which are curved or bowed outward like the sides of a cushion.

(''d'') ''Naut.'', ''pl.'', pieces of soft wood covered with tarred canvas, placed under the eyes of the rigging to prevent chafing from the sharp edge of the trestletrees. (''e'') A part of a bridge intervening between the truss and the masonry. (''f'') In ''cutlery'', the part of such instruments and tools as knives, chisels, etc., which adjoins the end of the handle; also, a metallic plate on the end of a pocket-knife handle. (''g'') In ''gun.'', a block of wood on the carriage of a siege-gun, upon which the breech of the gun rests when it is moved. (''h'') In ''arch.'', same as ''baluster'', 2. (''i'') In ''music'', the raised ridge which holds the tuning-pins of a piano. (''j'') A cap-piece or short timber placed at the top of a post as a bearing for a string-piece. (''k'') A perforated wooden block upon which sheet-metal is placed to be punched. (''l'') A sleeve-bearing through which a spindle passes. (''m'')}}
{{img float|file=century v01 p0641 c1f1.png|width=233px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Wagon-bolster. ''a'', axle-bar; ''b'', bolster.}} {{smaller|In ''stone-sawing'', one of the loose wooden blocks against which the ends of the pole of the saw rest. (''n'') A bar placed transversely over the axle of a wagon or in the middle of a car-truck to support the body. (''o'') One of the transverse pieces of an arch-centering, extending between the ribs and sustaining the voussoirs during construction.—'''Bob at the bolster.''' Same as ''cushion-dance''.—'''Compound bolster''', in ''car-building'', a bolster formed of timbers stiffened by vertical iron plates.}}}}

'''bolster''' (bōl′stėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''bolster'', ''n.'']   '''1.''' To support with a bolster.
{{smaller block|<poem>Suppose I ''bolster'' him up in bed,
And fix the crown again on his brow?</poem>
{{right|''R. H. Stoddard'', The King is Cold.}}}}

'''2.''' To prop; support; uphold; maintain: generally implying support of a weak, falling, or unworthy cause or object, or support based on insufficient grounds: now usually with ''up'': as, to ''bolster up'' his pretensions with lies.
{{smaller block|O Lord, what bearing, what ''bolstering'' of naughty matters is this in a Christian realm!
{{right|''Latimer'', 5th Serm. bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}}}
{{smaller block|Persuasions used to further the truth, not to ''bolster'' error.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Pol., iii. § 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Still farther to appropriate and confirm the exciting narrative of this forgery, he had artfully ''bolstered'' it ''up'' by an accompanying anecdote.
{{right|''I. D’Israeli'', Amen. of Lit., II. 416.}}}}

'''3.''' To furnish with a bolster in dress; pad; stuff out with padding.
{{smaller block|Three pair of stays ''bolstered'' below the left shoulder.
{{right|''Tatler'', No. 245.}}}}

'''bolstering''' (bōl′stėr-ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''bolster'', ''v.'']   A prop or support; padding.

'''bolster-work''' (bōl′stėr-wėrk), ''n.'' Architectural features, or courses of masonry, which are curved or bowed outward like the sides of a cushion.

''bolt'' (only in the first sense: twice in glosses, “''catapultas'', speru, ''boltas'',” to which is due, perhaps, the erroneous suggestion that AS. ''bolt'' is a reduced form of L. Teut. word with the primary meaning of ‘arrow’ or ‘missile.’]   '''1.''' An arrow; especially, in ''archery'', the arrow of a crossbow, which was short and thick as compared with a shaft.
{{smaller block|A fool’s ''bolt'' is soon shot. {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iii. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The infidel has shot his ''bolts'' away,
Till, his exhausted quiver yielding none,
He gleans the blunted shafts that have recoil’d,
And aims them at the shield of truth again.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, vi. 873.}}}}
'''2.''' A thunderbolt; a stream of lightning: so named from its apparently darting like a bolt.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''bolts'' that spare the mountain side
His cloud-capt eminence divide,
And spread the ruin round.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', tr. of Horace, Odes, ii. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Harmless as summer lightning plays
From a low, hidden cloud by night,
A light to set the hills ablaze,
But not a ''bolt'' to smite. ''Whittier'', Kenoza Lake.</poem>}}
'''3.''' An elongated bullet for a rifled cannon.—'''4.''' A cylindrical jet, as of water or molten glass.—'''5.''' A metallic pin or rod, used to hold objects together. It generally has screw{{img float|file=century v01 p0641 c2f2.png|width=129px|align=left|cap={{smaller|''a'', carriage-bolt; ''b'', tire-bolt; ''c'', wagon-skein bolt.}}}} threads cut at one end, and sometimes at both, to receive a nut.—'''6.''' A movable bar for fastening a door, gate, {{img float|file=century v01 p0641 c2f3.png|width=235px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Door-bolt.}}}} window-sash, or the like; specifically, that portion of a lock which is protruded from or drawn back within the case by the action of the key, and makes a fastening by being shot into a socket or keeper.—'''7.''' An iron to fasten the legs of a prisoner; a shackle.

[[File:century v01 p0641 c2f1.png|center|265px]]
{{c|{{smaller|1, Double-headed bolt. 2, Eye-bolt. 3, Lewis bolt. ''a'', head; ''b'', shank; ''c'', washer; ''d'', nut; ''e'', ''e'', pieces secured by the nut to the object ''f''; ''g'', collar; ''i'', barbed shank surrounded by lead, ''k''.}}}}

{{smaller block|Away with him to prison, lay ''bolts'' enough upon him.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1.}}}}

'''8.''' In ''firearms'': (''a'') In a needle-gun, the sliding piece that thrusts the cartridge forward into the chamber and carries the firing-pin. {{smaller|It has a motion of rotation about its longer axis for the purpose of locking the breech-mechanism before firing.}} (''b'') In a snap-gun, the part that holds the barrel to the breech-mechanism.—'''9.''' A roll or definite length of silk, canvas, tape, or other textile fabric, and also of wall-paper, as it comes from the maker ready for sale or use.

<poem>''Face.'' Where be the French petticoats,
And girdles and hangers?
''Sub.'' Here, in the trunk,
And the ''bolts'' of lawn.   ''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, v. 2.</poem>
'''10.''' A bundle. (''a'') Of straw, a quantity loosely tied up. Also ''bolting'' or ''bolton.'' (''b'') Of osier rods, a quantity bound up for market, 3½ feet around the lower band. (''c'') Of reeds, one of 3 feet in circumference. [Eng.]—'''11.''' The closed ends of leaves of an uncut book which present a double or quadruple fold.—'''12.''' The comb of a bobbin-net machine on which the carriages move.—'''13.''' In ''wood-working'': (''a'') A mass of wood from which anything may be cut or formed. (''b'') Boards held together, after being sawed from the log, by an uncut end or stub-shot.—'''14†.''' A name for certain plants, as the globe-flower and marsh-marigold.—'''15.''' [In this and the next sense from the verb.] The act of running off suddenly; a sudden spring or start: as, the horse made a ''bolt.''
{{smaller block|The Egyptian soldiers, as usual, made an immediate ''bolt'', throwing away their arms and even their clothes.
{{right|''E. Sartorius'', In the Soudan, p. 65.}}}}
'''16.''' In ''politics'', the act of withdrawing from a nominating convention as a manifestation of disapproval of its acts; hence, refusal to support a candidate or the ticket presented by or in the name of the party to which one has hitherto been attached; a partial or temporary desertion of one’s party. [U. S.]—'''17.''' The act of bolting food.—{{smaller|'''Barbed bolt,''' a bolt with points projecting outward, which bear against or enter into the surrounding material, and thus prevent its withdrawal.—'''Bolt and shutter,''' in ''clock-making'', an adjustment of a spiral spring in a turret clock, such that while the clock is winding there may be another spring in action to prevent}} a stoppage of the works.—'''Bolt and tun,''' in ''her.'', a term applied to a bird-bolt in pale piercing through a tun.—'''Bringing-to bolt,''' a bolt with an eye at one end and a screw-thread and nut at the other, used in drawing parts toward each other.—'''Chain-plate bolt.''' Same as ''chain-bolt.''—'''Copper bolt.''' See ''copper bit'', under ''bit''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Countersunk bolt,''' a bolt having its head beveled and set into a corresponding cavity in one of the parts which it connects.—'''Dormant bolt,''' a door-bolt operated by a special key or knob.—'''Key-head bolt,''' a bolt with a projection from the chamfer of its head to hold it so that it will not revolve with the nut.—'''Liphead bolt,''' a bolt of which the head projects sidewise.—'''Roller bolts,''' in ''coach-building'', the bolts on the splinter-bar to which the traces are attached.

'''bolt<sup>1</sup>''' (bōlt), ''v.''   [= Sc. ''boult, bout, bowt''; < ME. ''bolten, bulten'' (in the latter form varying in one instance with ''pulten'', mod. E. ''pelt''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.), spring, start, also fetter, shackle (= MHG. ''bulzen'', go off like an arrow); the other senses are modern, all being derived from ''bolt''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', in its two main senses of ‘missile’ and ‘pin for fastening’: see ''bolt''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To go off like a bolt or arrow; shoot forth suddenly; spring out with speed and suddenness: commonly followed by ''out'': as, to ''bolt out'' of the house.
{{smaller block|<poem>Angry Cupid, ''bolting'' from her eyes,
Hath shot himself into me like a flame.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>This Puck seems but a dreaming dolt, . . .
And oft out of a bush doth ''bolt''.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Nymphidia.}}}}
'''2.''' To spring aside or away suddenly; start and run off; make a bolt.
{{smaller block|Stage-coaches were upsetting in all directions, horses were ''bolting'', boats were overturning, and boilers were bursting. {{right|''Dickens.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The gun, absolutely the most useless weapon among us, could do nothing, even if the gunners did not ''bolt'' at the first sight of the enemy. {{right|''O’Donovan'', Merv, x.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''politics'', to withdraw from a nominating convention as a means of showing disapproval of its acts; hence, to cease to act in full accord with one’s party; refuse to support a measure or candidate adopted by a majority of one’s colleagues or party associates. [U. S.]
{{smaller block|Mr. Raymond agreed, . . . after some hesitation, but with the understanding that, if it [the Philadelphia Convention of 1868] fell under the control of the Copperheads, he would ''bolt''. {{right|''The Nation'', VI. 2.}}}}
'''4†.''' To fall suddenly, like a thunderbolt. {{smaller block|<poem>As an eagle
His cloudless thunder ''bolted'' on their heads.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 1696.}}}}
'''5.''' To run to seed prematurely, as early-sown root-crops (turnips, etc.), without the usual thickening of the root, or after it.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To send off like a bolt or arrow; shoot; discharge.—'''2.''' To start or spring (game); cause to bolt up or out, as hares, rabbits, and the like.
{{smaller block|<poem>Jack Ferret, welcome. . .
What canst thou ''bolt'' us now? a coney or two</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', New Inn, iii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To expel; drive out suddenly.
{{smaller block|<poem>To have been ''bolted'' forth,
Thrust out abruptly into Fortune’s way,
Among the conflicts of substantial life.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, iii. 77.}}}}
'''4.''' To blurt out; ejaculate or utter hastily.—'''5.''' To swallow hurriedly or without chewing: as, to ''bolt'' one’s food.
{{smaller block|These treacherous pellets are thrown to the bear, who ''bolts'' them whole. {{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXX. 39.}}}}
'''6.''' [After I., 3.] In ''politics'', to break away from and refuse to support (the candidate, the ticket, or the platform presented by or in the name of the party to which one has hitherto adhered); leave or abandon: as, to ''bolt'' the presidential candidate.
{{smaller block|A man does not ''bolt'' his party, but the candidate or candidates his party has put up. Sometimes, though less properly, he is said to ''bolt'' the platform of principles it has enunciated. The essential point is, that the bolter does not necessarily, in fact does not usually, abandon the political organization with which he is connected. He not infrequently votes for some men upon its ticket, and at the same time ''bolts'' others by “scratching” their names.{{right|''N. Y. Evening Post'', Aug. 20, 1887.}}}}
'''7.''' To fasten or secure with a bolt or an iron pin, as a door, a plank, fetters, or anything else.—'''8.''' To fasten as with bolts; shackle; restrain.
{{smaller block|<poem>It is great
To do that thing that ends all other deeds;
Which shackles accidents, and ''bolts'' up change.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>That I could reach the axle, where the pins are
Which ''bolt'' this frame; that I might pull them out.</poem>{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To bolt a fox''', in ''fox-hunting'', when a fox has run to earth, to put a terrier into the hole, and, when he is heard barking, to dig over the spot from which the sound proceeds, and so get at the fox.}}

'''bolt'''<sup>1</sup> (bōlt), ''adv.''   [< ''bolt''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'' or ''v.'']   '''1.''' Like a bolt or arrow: as, “rising ''bolt'' from his seat,” ''G. P. R. James.''
{{smaller block|There she sat ''bolt'' upright!{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 266.}}}}
'''2.''' Suddenly; with sudden meeting or collision.
{{smaller block|[He] came ''bolt'' up against the heavy dragoon.{{right|''Thackeray.''}}}}

'''bolt'''<sup>2</sup> (bōlt), ''v. t.''   [Early mod. E. also ''boult'', ''bowlt'', ''boolt'', Sc. ''bout'', ''bowt''; < ME. ''bulten'', < OF. ''bulter'', earlier ''buleter'' (mod. F. ''bluter''; ML. reflex ''buletare'') for *''bureter'' (= It. ''burattare''), sift, < *''buret'', ''burete'', ''burate'', a coarse woolen cloth (cf. dim. ''buretel'', ''burtel'', mod. F. ''bluteau'' = It. ''burattello'', a bolter, meal-sieve: see ''boul-''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
